frameworks.name: 10x Litmus Test for Opportunity Attention
frameworks.definition: A heuristic for filtering which opportunities deserve a founder's dedicated time: the projected outcome must be at least 10x the current business size; below that threshold, the opportunity cost of attention is not justified.

frameworks.name: No Half Measures Commitment Framework
frameworks.definition: A decision doctrine stating that partial commitment is functionally equivalent to no commitment; when pursuing any meaningful goal, all alternatives must be eliminated to guarantee full effort.

frameworks.name: Irreversibility Filter
frameworks.definition: A pre-decision screening step that identifies which categories of action are irreversible (reputation damage, capital loss above a threshold, time lost) and excludes them from risk-taking, reserving bets only for domains with recoverable downside.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses a 10x minimum threshold to decide which opportunities deserve dedicated attention: at a base of ~$100M, an opportunity must project to at least $1 billion before he commits meaningful time to it. Below that threshold, the opportunity cost of founder attention is not justified.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder already operating a business at meaningful scale (Hormozi's context: ~$100M baseline)
claims.mechanism: At large existing scale, the absolute cost of founder attention is high; only opportunities large enough to move the needle relative to current size justify the opportunity cost of redirection.

numbers.axis: minimum required projected outcome to justify dedicated founder attention

bounded_by: Threshold scales with current business size; a founder at $1M baseline uses a different absolute number
Does not apply to exploratory experiments that require minimal time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies reputation damage as the single most irreversible category of risk a founder faces: you cannot bankrupt yourself out of a bad reputation the way you can recover from financial loss, making any bet with pure reputational downside categorically different from financial bets.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Financial losses are bounded and recoverable through time and reinvestment; reputational losses are unbounded and compound negatively because trust, once broken publicly, cannot be repurchased.
bounded_by: Taking a stance on a controversial cause that repels one audience and attracts another is a trade-off, not a pure reputational risk, because it moves you toward a different group rather than simply destroying trust

claims.text: Alex Hormozi draws a distinction between reputational trade-offs and reputational risks: publicly supporting a cause that alienates some audiences while attracting others is a trade-off (net-neutral or net-positive in long-run), whereas actions that only destroy trust with no compensating upside are true reputational risks that must be avoided entirely.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A trade-off reallocates audience composition without destroying total trust capital; a pure risk destroys trust capital with no offsetting gain.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi holds that time is the only non-replenishable resource, and that every moment spent on any activity carries the opportunity cost of the highest-return alternative use of that time; people who compound better trades for their time end up with more of everything else.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Time is finite and non-fungible; allocating it to a lower-return activity structurally prevents capture of the higher-return alternative, creating a compounding divergence over years between those who trade time well and those who don't.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that certain bets offer high return with low risk simultaneously, using the example of a billionaire accumulating nickels whose metal content exceeds face value: when the government removes the coin from currency, the investor melts the nickels for a 40% gain with no realistic downside. Hormozi frames this as the target shape for any large capital deployment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Bet requires identifying an asymmetric situation where the downside is capped (at worst, retain the original capital) and the upside is credible

numbers.axis: projected upside on nickel-metal arbitrage bet

bounded_by: This specific example was attributed to a Tony Robbins story, not Hormozi's own investment; the principle is illustrative rather than prescriptive

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when facing two viable paths, a capital bet that would expose a material percentage of net worth or existing capital to loss is categorically inadvisable, regardless of projected upside, because it violates the principle of not betting the empire for a pot of gold.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Decision involves committing a significant share of existing net worth or operational capital
Alternative paths with lower capital risk exist
claims.mechanism: Betting a high share of existing capital on a single outcome converts a recoverable downside into an existential one, eliminating the optionality required to take future bets.
bounded_by: The quote Hormozi attributes to Charon Srivatsa: 'You bet what you have and need for something you don't have and don't need — it's never a good bet'

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that partial commitment to any significant goal is functionally equivalent to no commitment: being half-in gives people the emotional sensation of progress while providing no actual probability of winning, and is therefore worse than either a full commitment or a clean exit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Half-commitment allocates effort below the threshold required for success while maintaining enough engagement to prevent the person from redirecting effort elsewhere, producing the worst-case outcome: effort spent, result missed.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that going all-in on a decision is most reliable when you eliminate the possibility of reversing it: removing the exit option forces full commitment of cognitive and behavioral resources, which is the mechanism by which burning-the-boats strategies historically correlate with higher success rates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to large, long-horizon commitments where effort investment determines outcome
Does not apply to experimental short-cycle tests where pivoting is strategically valuable
claims.mechanism: Eliminating the retreat option removes the cognitive option-value of quitting, forcing the brain to invest fully in making the current path work rather than holding resources in reserve for an exit.
bounded_by: Making no bet guarantees a wrong outcome; making the bet with half-commitment also guarantees a wrong outcome; only full commitment preserves the possibility of success

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that first-time entrepreneurs facing a binary choice between a lower-risk path with higher success probability and a higher-risk path with higher upside should choose the lower-risk path, because the population of entrepreneurs who made large early bets and lost is far larger and less visible than the celebrated winners.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: First or early entrepreneurial venture (not a serial entrepreneur with recovered losses)
Both paths are genuine opportunities rather than one being clearly superior
claims.mechanism: Survivorship bias makes high-risk bets look attractive because failed bettors are invisible in the narrative; accounting for the full distribution shifts the expected value toward lower-risk paths for first-timers who lack the financial cushion and experience to recover from total loss.
bounded_by: Serial entrepreneurs with capital reserves and pattern recognition may have different risk calculus
Hormozi is describing his own current decision differently because he is not a first-timer

claims.text: Alex Hormozi describes his presentation flop at a personal trainer conference as evidence that mixing value delivery with a sales pitch in one session produces worse outcomes than either pure value delivery or a pure sales presentation: he delivered 3+ hours of genuine value and then rushed a 15-minute pitch, generating almost zero sales from an engaged audience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Audience had already received substantial free value in the same session
claims.mechanism: Mixing frames (value-giver vs. seller) in a single session creates cognitive dissonance in the audience: they entered as learners and are asked to switch to buyer mode without a clean transition, producing resistance rather than purchase intent.

numbers.axis: sales generated from a hybrid value-plus-pitch presentation

anchors.value: approximately 2 sales from a full conference audience

bounded_by: Hormozi frames this as his biggest-ever presentation flop, suggesting this was not a typical outcome under normal pitch conditions

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's rule for presentations and sales sessions is binary: either deliver pure value or sell — do not attempt to combine them in a single interaction, because blending the two produces the outcome of neither.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Live presentation or sales interaction where audience frame (learner vs. buyer) is established early

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that sales micro-skills (tone, pacing, humor, warmth) transfer directly to non-commercial persuasion contexts such as getting rule exceptions from staff or service workers, and that the underlying principle is getting the other person to want to do what you want rather than feeling obligated to comply.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Positive emotional state in the listener reduces the perceived cost of compliance; a person in a good mood will bend or interpret rules favorably, whereas a person in a neutral or negative mood applies them rigidly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi holds that a founder who makes a large swing at a big opportunity has an obligation to eliminate every controllable variable that could cause failure, so that any loss is attributable only to factors outside their control — this is framed as the only defensible way to take a large risk.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has decided to pursue the high-risk, high-upside path rather than the conservative path
claims.mechanism: Controllable variables represent avoidable probability mass on the failure side of the distribution; eliminating them shifts the expected outcome upward while preserving intellectual honesty about what was not in the founder's hands.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes, referencing Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends and Influence People, that a person's own name is their favorite word in any language, and that remembering and using someone's name in an unexpected meeting context provides significant social leverage by making the name-rememberer appear as the more prepared, attentive party.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: In-person or conference networking context where both parties may or may not remember each other
claims.mechanism: Asymmetric name recall creates an imbalance in perceived investment and attention; the party whose name was remembered feels valued and the other party feels socially indebted, shifting conversational leverage.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes a billionaire (sourced from a Tony Robbins story) who has been stockpiling nickels because the metal content (nickel alloy) is worth more than five cents per coin. The billionaire's thesis is that when the US government eventually demonetizes the nickel — which is economically rational because producing it costs more than its face value — he will melt his stockpile and realize approximately a 40% gain. In the meantime, he holds a liquid, capital-preserving asset with no downside beyond opportunity cost. Hormozi uses this to illustrate that high-return, low-risk bets exist and that finding them should be the goal of capital deployment decisions.

At a personal trainer conference, Alex Hormozi agreed to speak and prepared an exceptionally thorough presentation. After delivering more than three hours of high-quality tactical content, he compressed what would have been a 90-minute sales webinar into a rushed 15-minute soft pitch, delivering the offer price without conviction or proper framing. Despite the strong value delivered earlier, he closed approximately two sales from a full conference room. He describes this as the biggest presentation flop of his career, attributing the failure to trying to blend the value-giver frame with the seller frame in a single session — a 'half measure' that failed both objectives.

Outside a restaurant in San Diego, Alex Hormozi asked the hostess (Amy) about the dress code while wearing casual attire. Rather than arguing or making demands, he engaged her warmly by name, acknowledged the situation with humor, and asked for permission rather than making demands. She cleared his entry with the restaurant. He uses this as evidence that sales micro-skills (tone, warmth, getting people into a good mood before asking) transfer directly from commercial sales into everyday social interactions.

Arriving at an ice cream shop just as it was closing, Alex Hormozi called ahead, opened with humor about being in the 'doghouse,' and asked for a small exception with high energy and a commitment to be fast. The shop kept its doors open for him and his wife. He describes this as another application of the same micro-skill set: get the person in a positive emotional state, make the ask feel low-cost and rewarding for them to grant, and frame yourself as the kind of person whose presence will be a positive experience.

At the Reels conference for real estate agents in San Diego, Alex Hormozi encountered a man who told him his productivity insight was that he got more done when he cut back on watching Netflix while working. Hormozi catalogued multiple layers of dysfunction in this statement: (1) the person was watching Netflix at all during work, (2) they framed this as a discovery rather than an obvious baseline, and (3) they said they 'cut back' rather than committing to stop. He uses this as an illustration of how half-measures and partial commitments can be dressed in the language of progress while representing the opposite.

practices.text: When making a major multi-year decision, change your physical environment — particularly travel by plane — to gain literal and psychological distance from the everyday context that anchors your thinking.

Before committing to a large irreversible bet, run the Irreversibility Filter: ask whether the downside involves reputation damage, loss of a critical share of net worth, or unrecoverable time. If yes to any, do not make the bet.
When going all-in on a commitment, structure it so that reversing the decision is practically impossible — eliminate the exit option as a way to force full cognitive and behavioral commitment.

Measure success in any endeavor by whether you completed the actions that would make failure unreasonable given the circumstances, not by whether you achieved the outcome — outcomes have variance, but action execution is within your control.
In any networking or persuasion context, use the other person's name deliberately and early; it is the word they respond to most positively and shifts leverage in your favor.

When preparing a keynote or presentation for an audience that knows more than you on their domain, position yourself around a complementary angle (e.g., how you would approach winning if you were starting fresh in their field) rather than competing on their domain knowledge.
